subject: Using same covariates in a distance sampling model and subsequent model

messages.author: a8e868120fe0b59e
messages.subject: Using same covariates in a distance sampling model and subsequent model
parts:
Hello,

I have a question about if it is appropriate to use some of the same covariates in both an abundance estimation model and a subsequent environmental model. 

In my study, I am using NEON avian point count surveys to see how environmental variables impact community diversity (species richness, functional diversity etc. ). I first correct for each species' incomplete detection using a distance sampling model. I then take those corrected species-level abundances, calculate community diversity metrics, and model community diversity against environmental covariates. 

My bayesian distance sample model has an "abundance model" that uses covariates of latitude and elevation. However, I also use latitude and elevation to model community diversity in my environmental model too, but I am uncertain if reusing these two variables in both sets of models will bias the estimates somehow. 

I came across a related posting on this forum, but it was about using the same covariates in both the abundance and detection model, rather than between the abundance model of the distance sampling and a subsequent environmental model:
https://groups.google.com/g/unmarked/c/fL9QOXu_PLs?pli=1 

If anyone has any thoughts, or links to papers that test this/use a similar approach, I'd greatly appreciate the help!

Best,
-Colin

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Using same covariates in a distance sampling model and subsequent model
parts:
Dear Colin,

thanks for that question: to me, this is one of the 24 Open Research Questions in hierarchical modellingology in ecology. I have often wondered about it.

I feel that using the same covariate first in a model to estimate N or z, and then also in a second-step analysis where we treat the estimate of N or z as a response, and include in the set of explanatory variables the same covariate, is somewhat circular (apologies for the long sentence....). However, if some covariate is important to explain variation in N or z, then we would want to have it in the first step of the analysis, since to get good estimates of N or z, we don't want a mis-specified model. Looks like a conundrum.

I assume that a more mathy spirit could address the question of what to do best in this situation in an analytical manner. But for common people like us I'd say what I always say when I fail to understand something in stats: Simulation is the answer. That would result in a really interesting paper indeed.

Best regards  --- Marc

messages.author: bed9858844040a0b
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Using same covariates in a distance sampling model and subsequent model
parts:
Ideally, I would integrate all of this with a community abundance model. If you model abundance for each species as a function of community hyper-parameters, you can put your covariates of interest on abundance, and then derive diversity relationships with those covariates. Admittedly, however, community models can get computationally unwieldy with large datasets, although you would then get the benefit of being able to include species with relatively little data in your diversity estimates.

I suppose if you're far enough along in the project, it might be too late to backtrack, but in that case, you might expect the same principles to apply. If you've already put latitude and elevation in your abundance models, those relationships should be reflected in your abundance estimates. So, I guess if you fit latitude and elevation relationships with diversity derived from your abundance estimates, you are in a sense deriving the estimated relationships that already exist in the abundance estimates, which seems OK, except that you presumably wouldn't have rare species represented for which you were not able to fit abundance models.

parts:
Thanks all for your input! 

Quresh, to address your suggestions about community estimation, I have adapted models by Sollmann et al (2015) to estimate rare species using community hyper parameters in my distance sampling models (https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.12518). However, the result or this model was still individual species abundance estimates that I then used to calculate community diversity metrics. You seem to suggest that I somehow integrate the covariates from the community diversity model and input them directly into a second model (if I am following your logic)? Not sure if I understood correctly or not, but seems like an intriguing approach. 

Marc, a simulation study would indeed be interesting! Maybe one day I'll have the time, haha. It's at least comforting to know that I haven't missed that paper being published and people are still discussing these issues. 

Appreciate the input!
-Colin

messages.author: bed9858844040a0b
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Using same covariates in a distance sampling model and subsequent model
parts: If you put the covariates on each species abundance in the first model (hierarchical distance sampling model) and have covariate effects be drawn from community-level hyper-parameters (just like the intercept), you can then derive covariate relationships with diversity from that model without the need for running a second model. The first model would in effect already describe covariate relationships with diversity as an emergent property of species level covariate relationships, so you would then just need to derive the relationships with diversity by calculating predicted diversity at different values of covariates included in the model. This is the usual way of doing things with these hierarchical community models (as far as I am aware). A major advantage of hierarchical models is integration to avoid the need for staged analyses. It looks to me that Sollmann et al. did indeed include covariates on species level abundance models within their community model. This is the approach I think you'd want unless I'm missing something unique to your study or data.
